title: Landlord Rights and Responsibilities in India: A Practical Guide for Owners
seoTitle: Landlord Rights and Responsibilities in India
description: What a landlord in India is genuinely entitled to, what they owe a tenant in return, and why the paperwork protects the owner more than anyone else.
excerpt: Most Indian landlords are one person with one flat and a loan, not an institution. Here is what you are actually entitled to, what you owe, and why the condition report is the owner's evidence.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: We have been on both sides of the agreement

hero.alt: Futuristic illustration of a key handover beneath a holographic balance scale weighing a home against a document

sources.label: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs — the Model Tenancy Act, 2021
India Code — central legislation, including the Registration Act, 1908 and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Government of Tamil Nadu — tenancy registration under the state's 2017 tenancy law

faq.q: Can I enter my own flat whenever I want?
faq.a: Not while it is let. You own the property, but for the term of the tenancy the tenant has possession of it, and having handed that over you do not get to disturb it at will. Keeping a spare key is normal; using it while the tenant is out is not. The clean solution is a single clause in the agreement allowing entry on prior notice and consent, with an exception for genuine emergencies such as fire or a burst pipe. Where a state has enacted a tenancy law based on the Model Tenancy Act, advance written notice may be a legal requirement rather than a courtesy.

faq.q: The rent is two months overdue. Can I cut the water and electricity or change the locks?
faq.a: No, and it is the single worst move available to you. Indian law protects settled possession — a person in occupation cannot be dispossessed by force, and someone thrown out that way can go to court to recover possession even against the owner. Cutting off essential services to make staying unbearable is treated as coercion rather than a utilities decision, and a lockout or intimidation can become a police matter rather than a civil one. You would be converting a case you would probably win into a case you can lose, while the arrears keep running. Go the written notice route instead.

faq.q: How much notice do I have to give to end a tenancy?
faq.a: There is no national answer. Tenancy is a State subject in India, so notice periods, the grounds on which possession can be recovered and the process all depend on your state's law and on your agreement. Many states still operate older rent-control statutes that apply only to certain buildings, rents or areas. Read your termination clause first, then check what your state has actually enacted — do not rely on a figure quoted in an article, including this one.

faq.q: Is it legal to refuse tenants who are bachelors, single women, non-vegetarian or of a particular religion?
faq.a: The honest legal position is that India has no general statute stopping a private owner from choosing a tenant on these grounds the way housing discrimination law works in some other countries, and constitutional equality guarantees operate mainly against the State. Some housing society rules have been criticised and challenged, and other laws apply in specific contexts such as caste-based exclusion. But the absence of a quick remedy is not approval — this platform does not endorse blanket bars, and they work against the owner too, because every category you exclude shrinks your pool, lengthens vacancy and weakens your position. Screen on ability to pay and on references instead.

faq.q: Should the agreement be eleven months, or registered?
faq.a: Under the Registration Act, 1908, read with the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, leases of immovable property from year to year or for a term exceeding one year require registration. That threshold is why the eleven-month agreement became the default across India. Stamp duty and registration charges are set by your state, and where a state has enacted its own tenancy law there may be a separate registration route with a rent authority. An unregistered document is a weaker instrument if you ever need to rely on it, so weigh the saving against what you are giving up.

faq.q: The tenant is disputing my deposit deductions. What decides it?
faq.a: Evidence, and almost always the evidence you failed to create on day one. If you have a signed condition report with dated photographs from handover, meter readings, and a written repair thread, the conversation is short. If you have none of that, you are the one making a claim about the state of the flat four years ago with the money already in your hand, and that is a weak position however right you are. Deduct only for genuine damage rather than fair wear, itemise every deduction with a number and preferably a bill, and refund the balance within the period the agreement states.

body:
Ravi owns one flat in Porur. He bought it in 2019 with a loan he is still paying, and he lets it out because the EMI does not pay itself.

In 2022 a tenant rang him on a Sunday about a dead geyser. Ravi was two states away at a wedding. He could easily have said Monday. Instead he called the plumber he had used for years, sent him across, and paid over UPI without seeing the invoice. Three thousand rupees and one phone call from a wedding hall.

That tenant stayed four years. Rent landed on the second of every month. When she moved out she had already repainted a wall she had scuffed herself, unasked, and handed him a WhatsApp thread with every repair either of them had ever done, in order, with dates.

His neighbour owns an identical flat one floor up. That one argues about every repair. His flat has been empty for five of the last thirty-six months.

Same asset, same building. One of them is running it like a business.

Written for owners. Tenants are welcome to read over the shoulder — you will see plainly what your landlord is entitled to, and where they are not.

## Most Indian landlords are one person with one flat

A lot of writing about renting assumes the landlord is a company with a legal department and a maintenance crew. In India that is rarely who you are dealing with. The typical owner has one property, often bought on a loan, sometimes inherited, frequently lives in another city, and treats rental income as a supplement rather than a business. No float to absorb three empty months, no lawyer on retainer.

That explains behaviour that reads as unreasonable from the other side of the door. An owner dragging his feet on a repair is sometimes stalling and sometimes genuinely short that month. An owner nervous about letting to a group of young men has usually heard one loud story from a friend and has nothing else.

## What you are genuinely entitled to

- **Rent on time and in full.** The date in the agreement is the date. You are not being difficult by expecting it.
- **The property back in reasonable condition**, allowing for fair wear and tear. A four-year tenancy leaves marks. That is use, not damage, and the difference is worth settling in your own head before you inspect anything.
- **Notice before the tenant leaves**, on whatever terms the agreement sets.
- **Reasonable use.** The flat used as agreed — as a residence if that is what it was let for, by the people you agreed to, without subletting or commercial use unless you consented.
- **Recourse against genuine damage.** A broken window, a burnt countertop, a door someone kicked in: properly deductible, itemised, with the cost evidenced.
- **Access for real reasons**, on notice — inspection, repairs, showing the place as the term winds down.
- **The right to end the tenancy** at the end of its term or on a genuine breach, through the proper route.
- **A rent revision at renewal.** Not mid-term. At renewal, in the open, as a conversation.

One honest caveat. Notice periods, the grounds for recovering possession and the process are set by your state and your agreement, not by any national rule — tenancy is a **State subject** in India. Anyone who says a landlord must give three months anywhere in India is guessing. Read your agreement, then check your state.

## What you owe in return

**Habitable premises.** Working plumbing, sound wiring, a roof that does not leak, sanitation, a door that locks. A flat with a seepage problem is not a cheaper flat, it is one you are partly failing to deliver — and the tenant knows it every day, which is why that tenancy ends early.

**Structural repairs.** The wall, the roof, the pipes behind the plaster, the fittings that came with the place. Daily wear is fairly the tenant's — bulbs, a clogged drain, damage they caused. The middle ground is where arguments live, which is why it belongs in the agreement as a rupee threshold, not a debate at 9pm.

**Essential services.** Water and electricity are not leverage. More on that below.

**Notice before entry, and privacy after it.** You own the flat; for the term the tenant occupies it. Having handed over possession you do not get to disturb it at will. Keeping a spare key is normal; using it while they are at work is not. One line in the agreement — entry on prior notice and consent, except in a genuine emergency such as fire or a burst pipe — prevents the commonest source of bad blood in Indian tenancies.

**The deposit back, promptly, with itemised deductions.** If you deduct, say what for, with a number and preferably a bill. "Painting and cleaning" as a flat figure is how a departing tenant becomes someone who tells everyone not to rent from you. The [mechanics of deposits and deductions](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) are worth reading in full.

**Receipts, and an honest description of what you are letting.** If maintenance is extra, say the number before the visit. Much of the [gap between advertised rent and real monthly cost](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) is disclosure, not dishonesty, and owners lose good tenants at the signing table over it.

## Screening tenants — and where preference becomes discrimination

You are entitled to be careful about who lives in a property you are still paying a loan on. Screening is not a dirty word. Screening on the wrong things is. What actually predicts a good tenancy:

1. **Can they pay?** Employment letter, salary slips or a few months of bank statements. Ask directly — it is a normal question and reasonable people expect it.
2. **Are they who they say they are?** Government ID, checked against the person in front of you.
3. **What did the last landlord think?** One call: did the rent come on time, how did the exit go. The most informative thing you can do, and most owners never do it.
4. **How many people, and for how long?** Not to police it, but so the agreement reflects reality.
5. **Pets, vehicles, work-from-home, guests.** Everything you fail to ask becomes an argument in month seven.

Blanket refusals of bachelors, of single women, of people who eat meat, of people of a particular religion or region are common in Indian cities. Sometimes they are the owner's, sometimes the housing society's, sometimes a broker applying a filter nobody asked for. This platform does not endorse any of them, and I am not going to pretend they are a matter of taste.

Two things, said once. India has no general statute stopping a private owner from choosing a tenant on these grounds the way housing discrimination law works elsewhere, and constitutional equality guarantees operate mainly against the State. Some society rules have been challenged, and other laws bite in specific contexts such as caste-based exclusion, but a quick, reliable remedy does not exist. Do not mistake the absence of a remedy for approval.

And the self-interested argument, which is the one that moves people: every category you exclude shrinks your pool. A smaller pool means longer vacancy, a weaker position, and a worse tenant chosen in a hurry because the EMI is due. Screen hard on what predicts payment and care. Screen on nothing else.

## The paperwork protects you more than it protects the tenant

A written agreement, an inventory and a condition report look like things tenants ask for to protect themselves. In practice they protect the owner more, because the owner is the one who later has to prove a claim. A tenant disputing a deduction only has to say the geyser was already broken. You need evidence that it worked.

**Sign a real agreement, not a downloaded template.** Rent, deposit, maintenance figure, term, escalation on renewal, notice period on both sides, repair split with a rupee threshold, entry clause, and what happens to the deposit and by when. The clause-by-clause version is [its own subject](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india).

**Understand the registration threshold.** Under the Registration Act, 1908, read with the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, leases of immovable property from year to year or for a term exceeding one year require registration. That is why the eleven-month agreement became the Indian default. Stamp duty and charges are set by your state, and where a state has its own tenancy law there may be a separate registration route with a rent authority. An unregistered document is a weaker instrument if you ever need to rely on it.

**Do a condition report on handover day.** Walk the flat with the tenant, photograph every room and every existing defect, note the electricity and water meter readings, list what is provided — geyser, fans, chimney, wardrobes — and both sign it or exchange it on WhatsApp so it carries a timestamp. Ninety minutes.

That signed report is your evidence that the geyser worked. Without it, four years later, it is your word against theirs and you will lose — you cannot prove a negative, and the deposit is already in your hand, which makes you the one making the claim.

**Take rent by bank transfer**, so the payment history lives somewhere other than your head, **and keep the repair thread** in writing. It doubles as your evidence of having met your own obligations.

## Setting rent and deposit: the arithmetic of an empty flat

Do the arithmetic on your own flat, not on a number a neighbour quoted. Suppose it lets at thirty thousand and you hold out for thirty-two. If that extra two thousand costs two months of vacancy, you have given up sixty thousand rupees to gain two thousand a month — back to even in two and a half years, assuming the tenant stays that long, and that is before two months of maintenance on an empty flat.

A slightly lower rent that fills the flat this month, to someone who stays three years, beats a headline number that leaves it dark until March. Vacancy is the largest cost in small-scale letting and it is almost invisible, because it never arrives as a bill.

Same with the deposit. Norms vary widely across Indian cities and there is no national rule. What is true everywhere is that a high deposit narrows your pool to people with a lot of idle cash, which is not the same set as people who pay reliably — and where a state has enacted a tenancy law based on the Model Tenancy Act, it may be capped anyway.

## Repairs, complaints and late rent without escalating

Most landlord and tenant relationships do not break over a betrayal. They break over three small things handled badly in a row.

**On repairs:** answer fast even when you cannot fix fast. "I have called the plumber, he comes Thursday" costs nothing and buys enormous goodwill. Silence turns an inconvenience into a grievance. If it is genuinely the tenant's to fix, say so once, plainly, with the clause, and move on.

**On money for repairs:** never let a tenant fix your item on the assumption they will be reimbursed, and never leave them guessing. Agree the amount in writing first. Most deposit fights start as an unrecorded repair.

**On late rent:** ring on day three, not day fifteen, and ask rather than accuse. Most late rent is a salary date, a hospital bill or a bank problem, and it resolves in a week if you have not spent that week escalating. Put any extension in a message. A pattern rather than an incident is a different conversation — still a written one, before it is anything else.

**On complaints about you:** read them as data. A tenant who reports seepage in March is doing you a favour the one who says nothing until they leave is not. One rule holds all of it together — put it in writing, keep it boring, never make it personal. The owners who end up in real disputes are the ones who let a repair become a matter of respect.

## Ending a tenancy properly

When a tenancy ends normally, the process is unglamorous. Agree a date. Inspect jointly against the condition report from day one. Note the meter readings, settle utility and society dues, return the deposit within the period the agreement states with deductions itemised. Collect the keys, and confirm the handover in a message so the date is not a matter of memory.

When it ends badly, everything depends on the route, and here I have to be blunt about the thing that ruins owners.

**A lockout is not a remedy. Cutting water or electricity is not a remedy. Removing a door or the tenant's belongings is not a remedy.** These are coercion. Indian law has long protected settled possession — a person in occupation cannot simply be dispossessed by force, and someone thrown out that way can go to court to recover possession even against the owner. Disconnecting essential services to make staying unbearable is treated as coercion dressed up as a utilities matter, and physical dispossession or intimidation can become a police matter rather than a civil one.

The proper route: written notice under the agreement, then a formal legal notice through a lawyer by registered post, then the Rent Authority or Rent Court if your state has enacted a tenancy law establishing one, otherwise the civil route. Slower than it should be, and the only route that ends with you holding the flat and the law on your side. If a tenant wants out mid-term, read the mechanics of [ending a lease early](/blog/breaking-a-lease-in-india) before you refuse — someone allowed to leave cleanly, with a replacement lined up, is better business than an occupied flat and a fight.

## The Model Tenancy Act, from the owner's side

In June 2021 the Union Cabinet approved the **Model Tenancy Act, 2021**, usually written about as a tenant-protection measure. Read from the other side it is at least as much an owner's law — decades of old rent-control statutes made owners so wary of letting that housing sat empty while people looked for homes.

The parts an owner should care about:

- A **Rent Authority** to register tenancy agreements, with a **Rent Court** and **Rent Tribunal** above it, so disputes get a dedicated forum instead of queueing behind everything else in the civil courts. For an owner trying to recover possession, that is the whole ballgame.
- **Caps on the security deposit** — two months' rent for residential premises, six for non-residential — a clear expectation instead of a negotiation.
- **Refund of the deposit when the tenant hands back the premises**: a duty, and also a defined moment that ends the argument.
- **Written notice before the landlord enters**, twenty-four hours in the model text — worth adopting whether or not it binds you.

Now the caveat that changes everything. **A model law is a template, not a law.** The centre circulated it so states could adopt it, adapt it or ignore it, because rental housing is a state subject. Until your state enacts its own tenancy legislation, none of the above binds anyone there. Several states have moved — Tamil Nadu passed its own tenancy law in 2017, before the model was published, and requires agreements to be registered with a rent authority. Many states still run older rent-control statutes that apply only to certain buildings, rents or notified areas.

So do not memorise the model. Find out what your state has enacted and whether it covers your tenancy — the state housing department, or the rent authority if one exists, will tell you faster than any article. The tenant's view of the same landscape is set out in [what tenants actually have and do not have](/blog/tenant-rights-in-india).

## What experience teaches

**Photograph the flat on handover day, every time.** Empty rooms, every defect, close up. Ninety minutes that settles damage, repairs and the deposit at once.

**Call the previous landlord.** One phone call outperforms every document a prospective tenant can produce.

**Verify who you are dealing with, both ways.** Tenants are warned about [rental fraud](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) constantly and owners rarely are, but forged IDs and advance-payment tricks run in both directions. Meet the person. See the original ID.

## Where StayOnMap fits, and where it does not

Plainly: a listing platform cannot enforce anyone's rights. We are not a party to your agreement and we hold nobody's money.

What it does do is let you list directly, with no brokerage, so the rent you agree is the rent you keep. Rent, deposit and maintenance are required fields, so whoever contacts you has already seen the numbers rather than turning up to argue about them on the landing. Renters reach you directly instead of through an intermediary applying filters you never asked for. There is an owner verification flow, which is admin judgement on the documents you submit rather than a guarantee about anyone — we would rather say that than dress it up. Fewer people in between, and the numbers visible before the visit.

## What to remember

You are entitled to rent on time, reasonable use, the flat back in fair condition, notice, and a proper route to recover possession. You owe habitable premises, structural repairs, uninterrupted services, notice before entry, and the deposit back promptly with deductions itemised.

Tenancy is a state subject. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 binds nobody until a state enacts it, and notice periods and eviction grounds come from your state and your contract. Find out where your state stands.

Screen hard on ability to pay and on references, and on nothing else. Do the paperwork, because it is your evidence, not theirs. And never reach for the locks or the meter — that is the one move that turns a case you would win into a case you can lose.

Ravi still owns exactly one flat in Porur. It has been empty for two months in seven years. He has never sent a legal notice, and he has never had to, which is not luck — it is a plumber's number, a signed condition report and a habit of answering the phone.
